The '''[[mining industry]] in India''' is a major economic activity which contributes significantly to the [[economy of India]]. The [[gross domestic product]] (GDP) contribution of the mining industry varies from 2.2% to 2.5% only but going by the GDP of the total industrial sector, it contributes around 10% to 11%. Even mining done on small scale contributes 6% to the entire cost of mineral production. Indian mining industry provides job opportunities to around 700 individuals.<ref name="cci">{{cite web|title=MINERAL AND MINING INDUSTRY IN INDIA January, 2010|url=http://www.cci.in/pdf/surveys_reports/mineral-mining-industry.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111216100748/http://www.cci.in/pdf/surveys_reports/mineral-mining-industry.pdf|archive-date=16 December 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

As of 2012, India is the largest producer of [[Mica#Sheet mica|sheet mica]], 2015 the fourth largest producer of [[iron ore]], [[alumina]], [[chromite]], and [[bauxite]] in the world. A [[coal]] and iron ore project is in the fifth largest reserve in the world. India's metal and mining industry was estimated to be $106.4 billion in 2010.<ref name="bbc.co.uk">{{cite news |title=India mining industry 'out of control' |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-india-18438622 |access-date=22 February 2021 |work=BBC News |date=14 June 2012 |archive-date=2 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190102143334/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-india-18438622 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Mining in India has been prominent since ancient times. The field is noted for significantly contributing to the economy of the nation. However, the mining in India is also infamous for [[Human rights|human rights violations]] and [[pollution|environmental pollution]]. The industry has been hit by several high-profile [[Mining scam in India|mining scandals]] in recent times.<ref name="bbc.co.uk"/>

==Introduction ==
The tradition of mining in the region is ancient and underwent modernization alongside the rest of the world as India has gained independence in 1947.<ref name=Khullar631/> The [[P. V. Narasimha Rao#Economic reforms|economic reforms of 1991]] and the 1993 National Mining Policy further helped the growth of the mining sector.<ref name=Khullar631/> India's minerals range from both [[metal]]lic and non-metallic types.<ref name=Khullar632-633/> The metallic minerals comprise [[ferrous]] and [[non-ferrous]] minerals, while the nonmetallic minerals comprise mineral [[fuel]]s, [[precious stone]]s, among others.<ref name=Khullar632-633>Khullar, 632-633฿</ref>

D.R. Khullar holds that mining in India depends on over 3,100 [[Mining|mine]]s, out of which over 550 are fuel mines, over 560 are mines for metals, and over 1970 are mines for extraction of nonmetals.<ref name=Khullar631>Khullar, 631</ref> The figure given by S.N. Padhi is: 'about 600 coal mines, 35 oil projects and 6,000 metalliferous mines of different sizes employing over one million persons on a daily average basis.'<ref name=padhi1019>Padhi, 1019</ref> Both [[open cast mining]] and [[underground mining]] operations are carried out and [[drilling]]/[[pump]]ing is undertaken for extracting liquid or gaseous fuels.<ref name=Khullar631/> The country produces and works with roughly 100 minerals, which are an important source for earning foreign exchange as well as satisfying domestic needs.<ref name=Khullar631/> India also exports [[iron ore]], [[titanium]], [[manganese]], [[bauxite]], [[granite]], and imports [[cobalt]], [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], [[graphite]] etc.<ref name=Khullar631/>

Unless controlled by other departments of the [[Government of India]], mineral resources of the country are surveyed by the [[Ministry of Mines (India)|Ministry of Mines]], which also regulates the manner in which these resources are used.<ref name=Ar_ch2_pg4>Annual Report (2007-2008), Ministry of Mines, chapter 4, page 4</ref> The ministry oversees the various aspects of industrial mining in the country.<ref name=Ar_ch2_pg4/> Both the [[Geological Survey of India]] and the [[Indian Bureau of Mines]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ibm.nic.in/|title=IBM website|access-date=31 October 2016|archive-date=31 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161031155531/http://ibm.nic.in/|url-status=live}}</ref> are also controlled by the ministry.<ref name=Ar_ch2_pg4/> [[Natural gas]], [[petroleum]] and atomic minerals are exempt from the various activities of the Indian Ministry of Mines.<ref name=Ar_ch2_pg4/>

==History==
[[File:Coal mine in Dhanbad, India.jpg|thumb|Indian coal production is the 3rd highest in the world according to the 2008 Indian Ministry of Mines estimates.<ref name=MoM_doc1/> Shown above is a coal mine in [[Jharkhand]].]]
[[File:India - Manganese Ore Shipment - DPLA - f095b54426226115056074e2adec8451.jpg|thumb|right|Mining of manganase in 1951]]

[[Flint]] was known and exploited by the inhabitants of the [[Indus Valley Civilization]] by the 3rd millennium BCE.<ref name=Biagi1856>Biagi, page 1856</ref> P. Biagi and M. Cremaschi of [[Milan University]] discovered a number of [[Harappa]]n [[Quarry|quarries]] in archaeological excavations dating between 1985 and 1986.<ref name=Biagi1857>Biagi, 1857</ref> Biagi (2008) describes the quarries: 'From the surface the quarries consisted of almost circular empty areas, representing the quarry–pits, filled with aeolian sand, blown from the [[Thar Desert]] dunes, and heaps of limestone block, deriving from the prehistoric mining activity. All around these structures flint workshops were noticed, represented by scatters of flint flakes and blades among which typical Harappan-elongated [[blade]] cores and characteristic bullet cores with very narrow bladelet detachments.'<ref name=Biagi1858>Biagi, 1858</ref> Between 1995 and 1998, [[Accelerator mass spectrometry]] [[radiocarbon dating]] of Zyzyphus cf. nummularia [[charcoal]] found in the quarries has yielded evidence that the activity continued into 1870-1800 BCE.<ref name=Biagi1860>Biagi, 1860</ref>

Minerals subsequently found mention in [[Indian literature]]. George Robert Rapp—on the subject of minerals mentioned in India's literature—holds that:

{{Blockquote|[[Sanskrit]] texts mention the use of [[bitumen]], [[rock salt]], [[orpiment|yellow orpiment]], [[chalk]], [[alum]], [[bismuth]], [[calamine]], [[realgar]], [[stibnite]], [[Potassium nitrate|saltpeter]], [[cinnabar]], [[arsenic]], [[sulphur]], [[yellow ochre|yellow]] and [[red ochre]], [[black sand]], and [[red clay]] in prescriptions. Among the metals used were [[gold]], [[silver]], [[copper]], [[mercury (element)|mercury]], [[iron]], [[iron ore]]s, [[pyrite]], [[tin]], and [[brass]]. [[Mercury (element)|Mercury]] appeared to have been the most frequently used, and is called by several names in the texts. No source for mercury or its ores has been located. Leading to the suggestion that it may have been imported.<ref name=Rapp>Rapp, 11</ref>}}

==Geographical distribution==

The distribution of minerals in the country is uneven and mineral density varies from region to region.<ref name=Khullar631/> D.R. Khullar identifies five mineral 'belts' in the country: The North Eastern Peninsular Belt, Central Belt, Southern Belt, South Western Belt, and the North Western Belt. The details of the various geographical 'belts' are given in the table below:<ref name=Khullar632>Khullar, 632</ref>

India has yet to fully explore the mineral wealth within its marine territory, mountain ranges, and a few states and regions e.g. [[Gadchiroli]] in Maharashtra, [[Gadchiroli|Assam]].<ref name=Khullar632/> 

Over the last three years, Gadchiroli has also emerged as a mining hub, on its way to becoming another steel hub of India. Companies such as Lloyd's Metal and Energy Limited, with mines operated by Thriveni Earthmovers, have been successful in navigating internal conflict to start mining operations in the region since 2021. They have also received a government push, which aims to establish the region as the steel hub of India by 2030.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-03-20 |title='Gadchiroli steel city to be bigger than Jamshedpur in coming years' |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/nagpur/gadchiroli-steel-city-to-be-bigger-than-jamshedpur-in-coming-years/articleshow/108635675.cms#:~:text=The%20quality%20of%20iron%20ore,off%20operations%20due%20to%20forests. |access-date=2024-07-05 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref> 

The Maharashtra government has been working on improving infrastructure in the region to make this a reality.<ref>{{Cite web |date=30 August 2020 |title=Ministry of Road Transport & Highways |url=https://pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1649747 }}</ref> The LMEL's current Surjagad Iron Ore Mines, currently operating  are set to reach a production capacity of 25 MTPA, with the foundations of the Integrated Steel Plant already underway. Another player, Surjagad Ispat, has already entered the region, and more are sure to follow. 

If this becomes a reality, India steel capacity will increase, reducing both cost and an overall dependency on steel imports from China.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Law |first=Abhishek |date=2024-04-14 |title=India looks to rehaul its steel import reporting mechanism |url=https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/india-looks-to-rehaul-its-steel-import-reporting-mechanism/article68061548.ece |access-date=2024-07-05 |website=BusinessLine |language=en}}</ref>

==Minerals==

Along with 48.83% [[arable land]], India has significant sources of [[coal]] (fourth-largest reserves in the world), [[bauxite]], [[titanium ore]], [[chromite]], [[natural gas]], [[diamond]]s, [[petroleum]], and [[limestone]].<ref name="CIA">{{cite web |title=CIA Factbook: India |work=CIA Factbook |date=September 2022 |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/india/ |access-date=24 January 2021 |archive-date=18 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210318202107/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/india |url-status=dead }}</ref> According to the 2008 Ministry of Mines estimates: 'India has stepped up its production to reach the second rank among the [[chromite]] producers of the world. Besides, India ranks 3rd in production of coal & [[lignite]], 2nd in [[barite]]s, 4th in iron ore, 5th in bauxite and [[crude steel]], 7th in manganese ore and 8th in [[aluminium]].'<ref name=MoM_doc1>[http://mines.nic.in/imsene.html ''India's Contribution to the World's mineral Production''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070823060003/http://mines.nic.in/imsene.html |date=23 August 2007 }} (2008), Ministry of Mines, Government of India. National Informatics Centre.</ref>

India accounts for 12% of the world's known and economically available [[thorium]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.world-nuclear.org/info/inf62.htm |title=Information and Issue Briefs - Thorium |publisher=World Nuclear Association |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061107083059/http://www.world-nuclear.org/info/inf62.htm |archive-date=7 November 2006 }}</ref> It is the world's largest producer and exporter of mica, accounting for almost 60 percent of the net mica production in the world, which it exports to the [[United Kingdom]], [[Japan]], [[United States of America]] etc.<ref name=Khullar_650-651>Khullar, 650-651</ref> As one of the largest producers and exporters of iron ore in the world, its majority exports go to Japan, [[Korea]], [[Europe]] and the [[Middle East]].<ref name=Khullar_638>Khullar, 638</ref> Japan accounts for nearly 3/4 of India's total iron ore exports.<ref name=Khullar_638/> It also has one of the largest deposits of manganese in the world, and is a leading producer as well as exporter of manganese ore, which it exports to Japan, Europe ([[Sweden]], [[Belgium]], [[Norway]], among other countries), and to a lesser extent, the United States of America.<ref name=Khullar_638-640>Khullar, 638-640</ref>

== Legal and constitutional framework ==
India is not a signatory to the [[Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative]] [EITI].<ref>{{cite web |title=A Little More Transparency at EITI Can Go a Long Way {{!}} Center For Glo… |url=http://international.cgdev.org/blog/little-more-transparency-eiti-can-go-long-way |website= |access-date=22 February 2021 |date=24 July 2013}}</ref> But, on national scale, there are legal and constitutional framework to manage the mineral sector:
* The policy level guidelines for mineral sector is given by the National Mineral Policy of 2008.<ref>{{cite web |title=Press Information Bureau |url=http://pib.nic.in/newsite/erelease.aspx?relid=36463 |website=pib.gov.in |access-date=22 February 2021 |archive-date=2 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190102143129/http://pib.nic.in/newsite/erelease.aspx?relid=36463 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Mining operations are regulated under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) [MMDR] Act of 1957.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://mines.nic.in/index.aspx?level=1&lid=80&lang=1 |title=Archived copy |access-date=24 July 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150315034256/http://mines.nic.in/index.aspx?level=1&lid=80&lang=1 |archive-date=15 March 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref> 
* The State Governments, as owners of minerals, grant mineral concessions and collect royalty, dead rent and fees as per the provisions of MMDR Act 1957.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://mines.nic.in/faq.html |title=Ministry of Mines |access-date=24 July 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130615021316/http://mines.nic.in/faq.html |archive-date=15 June 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> These revenues are held in the Consolidated Fund of State Government until the state legislature approves their use through budgetary processes.<ref>{{cite web |title=Press Information Bureau |url=http://pib.nic.in/newsite/erelease.aspx?relid=90707 |website=pib.gov.in |access-date=22 February 2021 |archive-date=2 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190102143137/http://pib.nic.in/newsite/erelease.aspx?relid=90707 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In a recent development, the Supreme Court has said that "Ownership of minerals should be vested with the owner of the land and not with the government."<ref>{{cite web |title=Ownership of mineral wealth lies with owner of land: SC - Hindustan T… |url=http://www.hindustantimes.com/India-news/NewDelhi/Minerals-belong-to-land-owner-not-state-SC/Article1-1092290.aspx |website=Hindustan Times |access-date=22 February 2021 |date=24 July 2013}}</ref>

The subject of ‘mineral regulation and development’ occurs at S.No. 23 of the State list in the VIIth schedule to the Constitution.  However, the Constitution circumscribes this power, by giving Parliament the power under S.No. 54 of the Central list in the VIIth schedule, to enact legislation, and to this extent, the States will be bound by the Central legislation.  The Mines and Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act 1957 is the main Central legislation in force for the sector.  The Act was enacted when the Industrial Policy Resolution 1957 was the guiding policy for the sector, and thus was aimed primarily at providing a  mineral concession regime in the context of the metal making public sector undertakings.  After the liberalization in 1991, a separate National Mineral Policy was promulgated in 1993 which set out the role of the private sector in exploration and mining and the MMDR Act was amended several times to provide for a reasonable concession regime to attract the private sector investment including FDI, into exploration and mining in accordance with NMP 1993.{{citation needed|date=November 2023}}

The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957  (MMDR Act 1957 in short) was enacted so as to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union. The Act has been amended in 1972, 1986, 1994 and 1999 in keeping with changes in the policy on mineral development. The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Amendment  Act, 1999, inter-alia, provides for (a) introduction of a new concept of reconnaissance operations distinct from prospecting; (b) delegation of  powers to the State Governments to grant mineral concessions for limestone; (c) granting of mineral concession in non-compact and non-contiguous areas; (d) liberalizing the maximum area limits for prospecting licences and mining leases; (e) empowering the State Governments to make rules to curb the [[illegal mining]] etc.{{citation needed|date=November 2023}}

The Act was amended in the year 2015  with the intention of removing discretion and introducing more transparency in the grant of mineral concessions. The amendments now made to the  MMDR Act, 1957 provide that mineral concessions will be granted only on the basis of bidding at an auction, for the prospecting stage or mining stage as the case may be.{{citation needed|date=November 2023}}

New Mineral (Auction) Rules notified in 2015 for the auction procedures. The Minerals (Evidence of Mineral Contents) Rules, also notified at the same time   specifies the technical requirements.{{citation needed|date=November 2023}}

==Issues with mining==

One of the most challenging issues in India's mining sector is the lack of assessment of India's natural resources.<ref name=Khullar632/> A number of areas remain unexplored and the mineral resources in these areas are yet to be assessed.<ref name=Khullar632/> The distribution of minerals in the areas known is uneven and varies drastically from one region to another.<ref name=Khullar631/> India is also looking to follow the example set by [[England]], Japan and [[Italy]] to recycle and use [[scrap iron]] for the ferrous industry.<ref name=Khullar659>Khullar, 659</ref>

The first National Mineral Policy was enunciated by the Government in 1993 for liberalization of the mining sector. The National Mineral Policy, 1993 aimed at encouraging the flow of private investment and introduction of state-of-the-art technology in exploration and mining.  In the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five-Year Plan, it was observed that the main factors responsible for lack of success of the Policy were procedural delays in the processing of applications for mineral concessions and the absence of adequate infrastructure in the mining areas. To go into the whole gamut of issues relating to the development of the mineral sector and suggest measures for improving the investment climate the Mid-Term Appraisal had proposed the establishment of a High Level Committee. Accordingly, the Government of India, Planning Commission, constituted a Committee on 14 September 2005. under the Chairmanship of Shri Anwarul Hoda, Member, Planning Commission. The committee made detailed recommendations on all of its terms of Reference in December 2006. Based on the recommendations of the High Level Committee, in consultation with State Governments, the Government replaced the National Mineral Policy, 1993 with a new National Mineral Policy on 13 March 2008.

Under the [[British Raj]] a committee of experts formed in 1894 formulated regulations for mining safety and ensured regulated mining in India.<ref name=padhi1019/> The committee also passed the 1st Mines act of 1901 which led to a substantial drop in mining-related accidents.<ref name=padhi1019/> The accidents in mining are caused both by man-made and natural phenomenon, for example, explosions and flooding.<ref name=padhi1020>Padhi, 1020</ref> The main causes for incidents resulting in serious injury or death are roof fall, methane gas explosion, coal dust explosion, carbon monoxide poisoning, vehicular accidents, falling/slipping and hauling related incidents.<ref name=padhi1021>Padhi, 1021</ref>

In recent decades, the mining industry has been facing issues of large scale displacements, resistance of locals - as reported by the Indian journalist Aditi Roy Ghatak in the magazine [http://www.dandc.eu/articles/220537/index.en.shtml D+C Development and Cooperation] -, human rights issues like indentured labour as reported by the ''[[List of Goods Produced by Child Labor or Forced Labor]]'' and environmental issues like pollution, corruption, deforestation and dangers to animal habitats.<ref>{{cite web |author=Nick Robins and Pratap Chatterjee |url=http://www.freewebs.com/epgorissa/ |title=Home - Environmental Protection Group, Orissa |publisher=Freewebs.com |access-date=2012-03-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111209175533/http://www.freewebs.com/epgorissa/ |archive-date=9 December 2011 |df=dmy-all }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.indiawaterportal.org/post/9431 |title=ENVIS Newsletter on Environment Problems of Mining |publisher=India Water Portal |date=2011-06-22 |access-date=2012-03-23 |archive-date=10 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120610065305/http://www.indiawaterportal.org/post/9431 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.indiaenvironmentportal.org.in/content/goas-mining-problems |title=Goa's mining problems |publisher=India Environment Portal |access-date=2012-03-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718072418/http://www.indiaenvironmentportal.org.in/content/goas-mining-problems |archive-date=18 July 2011 |df=dmy-all }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=P. == Corporate Social Responsibility Study ==

=== Background ===
Mining plays an important role in Indian industry, which contributes about 3% of the [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] in the 1990s, and about 2% of the [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] now.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.asianage.com/business/economy/091117/7-8-per-cent-contribution-of-mining-sector-in-gdp-can-create-25-million-jobs-in-india.html|title=7-8 per cent contribution of mining sector in GDP can create 25 million jobs in India|date=2017-11-09|work=asianage.com/|access-date=2018-02-27|archive-date=28 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228041700/http://www.asianage.com/business/economy/091117/7-8-per-cent-contribution-of-mining-sector-in-gdp-can-create-25-million-jobs-in-india.html|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Goa]], a state of India, has 1000 million tonnes of iron ore reserves and thereby has a strong mining industry. It exports about 30 million tonnes of iron ore annually.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.goadmg.gov.in/IronInfo.aspx|title=Iron Information|website=www.goadmg.gov.in|access-date=2018-02-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228041719/http://www.goadmg.gov.in/IronInfo.aspx|archive-date=28 February 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the early 21 century, the demand of iron ore from China increased in a dramatic speed, accordingly, the export of iron ore from Goa increased. Meanwhile, Indian government loosened the regulation on iron ore trading. These aspects, along with other factors like [[spot contract]], resulted in the doubled export of iron ore between 2005 and 2010.

In order to maintain the sustainability of mining, the Indian government set up a series of regulations included in Act of Parliament in 1987. According to Act of Parliament, mining companies had to obtain the lease for 20 years in maximum from the Indian Government, otherwise, their mining behaviors were not allowed.

=== CSR and Mineral Foundation of Goa ===
When it comes to the [[Corporate social responsibility (India)|corporate social responsibility]] (CSR), Indian government encouraged companies to take discrete corporate social actions.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Corporate Responsibility. Social Action, Institutions and Governance.|last=Ronny|first=Manos|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|year=2016}}</ref> According to [[Companies Act 2013]] of India, every company was required to invest 2% of their [[net profit]] in social program annually. Discrete corporate social actions means corporate social actions are not a part of the core strategy in companies, so companies are more likely to take social actions by setting up their own foundation.

Mineral Foundation of Goa (MFG) is a non-profit organization that founded by 16 mine operators on 12 December 2000.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://goamining.org/index.php/organisation/mfg|title=MFG|website=goamining.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2018-02-27|archive-date=28 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228041617/http://goamining.org/index.php/organisation/mfg|url-status=live}}</ref> The main purpose of MFG is to implement their social responsibility by helping communities and residents near the mining area in various ways. Their most common take was to invest in social and environmental projects, such as environmental sustainability, healthcare and educational support. For instance, MFG totally invested Rs. 10 [[crore]]s in environmental sustainability project between 2000 and 2010. In some ways, they contributed a lot to the society through these projects, such as creating ponds, donating books and equipment to the schools. However, MFG was unwilling to give further support to maintain their results. On the other hand, farmers preferred to receive money from mining companies, whereas mining companies wanted to provide technical assistance.

=== The Ban ===
In 2010, Shah Commission visited Goa, and soon they found several important facts that existed in Goa's mining industry. Some mining companies continued mining even if their leases were expired, some were mining outside the permissive mining area., some failed to maintain a required distance between [[overburden]] and irrigation canals. All aspects above resulted in the fact that the production of iron ore exceeded the allowable output by more than 15%. Based on these negative impacts caused by mining industry, the state government shut down all 90 iron ore mines in Goa.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nepia.com/insights/industry-news/indias-supreme-court-lifts-iron-ore-mining-ban/|title=India's Supreme Court Lifts Iron Ore Mining Ban|website=www.nepia.com|access-date=2018-02-27|archive-date=28 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228041720/http://www.nepia.com/insights/industry-news/indias-supreme-court-lifts-iron-ore-mining-ban/|url-status=live}}</ref> Later, the Supreme Court also gave a temporary ban on mining operations in Goa.

=== Result and Conclusion ===
The ban on the mining industry directly resulted in a huge loss of government revenue, which is up to Rs. 50,000 crores (8 billion dollars).<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/industry/indl-goods/svs/metals-mining/indian-economy-lost-rs-50000-crore-on-iron-ore-mining-ban/articleshow/44953539.cms|title=Indian economy lost Rs 50,000 crore on iron ore mining ban|last=Upadhyay|first=Anindya|date=2014-10-28|work=The Economic Times|access-date=2018-02-27|archive-date=28 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228103641/https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/industry/indl-goods/svs/metals-mining/indian-economy-lost-rs-50000-crore-on-iron-ore-mining-ban/articleshow/44953539.cms|url-status=live}}</ref> Furthermore, the mining ban also hit India's GDP in 2013 and 2014. It also caused social problems as people who lost their jobs were unwilling to take their former occupations, like fishing and farming.

This study shows that when the core strategy conflicts with corporate social responsibility, the social benefits created by companies will not guarantee companies' normal operations.<ref name=":0" /> In Goa's case, even though some mining companies and organizations, like MFG, took corporate social actions, most of the mining companies are more profit-oriented. Due partially to the lack of government documents and supervision, mine operators became more opportunistic, in other words, companies tended to take the risk of doing illegal things and gain more profit. Moreover, social actions may not be sufficient. Despite the fact that the water quality had somewhat improved, the concentration of iron ore in water was still unacceptable in some periods.

extract:
The mining industry in India is a major economic activity which contributes significantly to the economy of India. The gross domestic product (GDP) contribution of the mining industry varies from 2.2% to 2.5% only but going by the GDP of the total industrial sector, it contributes around 10% to 11%. Even mining done on small scale contributes 6% to the entire cost of mineral production. Indian mining industry provides job opportunities to around 700 individuals.
As of 2012, India is the largest producer of sheet mica, 2015 the fourth largest producer of iron ore, alumina, chromite, and bauxite in the world. A coal and iron ore project is in the fifth largest reserve in the world. India's metal and mining industry was estimated to be $106.4 billion in 2010.
Mining in India has been prominent since ancient times. The field is noted for significantly contributing to the economy of the nation. However, the mining in India is also infamous for human rights violations and environmental pollution. The industry has been hit by several high-profile mining scandals in recent times.
